Their should be regulations in place requiring electrical COOPs to actually pay residential solar customers a fair price for the excess power they produce. Solar is a large investment that currently is only offset by a tax credit. For me the credit is worthless as my earnings are not enough to even use it. I always take the standard deduction. Their should be a tax refund, not just credit to encourage residential solar installations. 

There should also be regulations that require either the rural electric COOP or any electric company to purchase electricity from a new or existing solar farm at the same rate they are charging for it. Their should also be some sort of state incentive to encourage building of solar power generation and require companies to connect and support solar farm installations. When we inquired about the connection of our planned solar facility we were told it would be too costly for them to install new supply lines to accept our generated power. This needs to be changed. Electric companies or generators should be required to accept the solar production despite the initial cost. 

There needs to be a change in rules concerning roads and Indian tribes. If a tribe pays the bill to have a road improved the county or state should be held responsible for maintaining it.

problem_water: Both water sources for the area of Oklahoma City are polluted by both industry and natural run off from yards and rivers. These include OG&E's natural gas/ coal fired plant near Lake Overholser and severe influxes of water into the Lake Hefner reservoir from northside sewer well feeds and natural runoff from sewer drainage.
problem_cause_water: Nitrogen blooms are caused each summer when diatoms and algeal blooms, impact the flavor and chemistry of water quality, dramatically, including containing parasites that can cause gastric distress.
problem_solve_water:
The City has done many things to offset the excess flora in the water, but filtration has continued to be a major issue since piping allows years of reintroduction to occur despite the use of strong reagents and better filtration methods.
 The eventual solutions would be to do a cleanout of theentire system, once Graphene technology allows the removal of live organisms that donot improve water and harm people. Some minerals can be supplimented once graphene filtration removes the major chemical sludge from lake sources. Introducing lakevegetation that naturally cleans lake water is another more expensive,but useful way to reduce bad organisms and chemicals. Both approaches must be researched in Oklahoma!
problem_land:

Some noxious species like Cockle burrs, Moon flower do not improve prairies, but can be attractive if not grown for stupid reasons.
We do have incredible wild flowers that should be saved from extinction like the White Bachelor's Stick Bouquet flower in Woodward area.

Goatheads ought to be banned, but certain ands and predators depend on them for food as their sickers contain protein rich seeds. So, thischoosing of species needs guidance even for red cedar!

problem_land: Expansion of cities and suburban areas overtaking native grassland and forests.  In Broken Arrow (New Orleans street, just east of Olive) they just bulldozed about a quarter-quarter section of treed hilly land and burned the trees.  They are now leveling it for a new subdivision.
problem_cause_land: Developers are working to meet the demands of more homes for upper middle class folks.  Unfortunately, the houses and streets will increase rain run-off and decrease water 'soak' into the ground.
problem_solve_land:
1. Require 'infill' of vacant lots first before development of virgin land.
2. Require demolition of derelict housing and commercial buildings to use the land for residential and multifamily living areas.
3. "Re-develop" the inner city areas to attract folks to those areas instead of clearing more rural lands.  
4. Revise tax laws and other restrictions that are negative incentives to re-developing the inner city areas.
5. Provide incentives for supporting commercial development in inner city areas (grocery stores, restaurants, etc.) that would provide the necessities so that local dwellers do not have to travel outside the area for needed items.
6. Provide higher support funding for new schools in the inner city area to attract more middle income families to grow those neighborhoods.
problem_infra:
Bridges:  The number of bridges that need replacing seems to be growing without much of a plan to get them repaired in a reasonable time frame.  More emphasis needs to be placed on them sooner and in a concise plan.
Roads:  State highways like 69, continue to go on with temporary improvements and inadequate funding to be fixed and/or replaced with new pavement.  It was ludicrous recently when the State passed the law requiring that one drive in the right hand lanes except to pass because it was obvious that none of the erudite lawmakers had ever driven Hwy 69 from Big Cabin to Pryor.  The washboard highway in that area would have jarred the fillings from their teeth if they stayed in the right lane!  And similar problems exist all the way south on 69.  It is my guess that other roads in the state are similarly damaged, but funding to fix them is not available.
problem_cause_infra: The use of the Turnpike Authority to run the main highways has past its usable lifetime.  The Authority now keeps building more turnpikes only because it can then increase its debt.  Once the debt is paid off, it would cease to exist.  By continuing to incur debt, the Authority makes itself a never ending, self-perpetuating business.
problem_solve_infra:
1.  Stop the Turnpike Authority from building any additional turnpikes.
2.  Shut down the Authority and transfer the debt to the State Highway Department.  Assimilate the Authority equipment and operating personnel into the State Highway Department.  Reduce Authority management staff as necessary to avoid duplication with State Highway Department personnel.  Have the State continue to operate the existing turnpikes at the current use rates to pay off the current debt.
3.  Once the current debt it paid off, freeze the turnpike fees at the current level to cover ongoing maintenance and provide added funding to the State Highway Dept.  
4.  Require the State Highway Department to survey all state highways, rate them based on condition, and provide a comprehensive plan for maintenance and replacement.
5.  Have the State Highway Dept partner with OU, OSU, and/or other universities to develop new standards for highway construction that would lead to longer life-spans for highways in Oklahoma given our particular ground, weather, and traffic conditions.  Using the same old construction standards to replace highways is only getting us new highways that deteriorate just as fast as the old ones. 
6. To reduce maintenance costs, consider reducing the highway ROW mowing efforts.  Is there any purpose to the mowing other than the aesthetic value?  If not, then save the money and let the grasses grow.  Or just mow one car-width off each side and leave the rest of the ROW alone.

problem_land: It is my understanding that more land is privately owned than publicly owned, yet private landowners (myself included) do not often consider that they play a role in the maintenance and stewardship of these resources. It is not that people are deliberately poor stewards, it is just that the don't even consider stewardship in terms of those resources you're examining.
problem_cause_land: I believe simply that lack of education/knowledge contributes or clouds the issue. Having lived in Oklahoma most of my life and owned property or had family/friends who own property conservation of resources and the impact of how we use that property in those regards is not something often considered - it's just not on the radar.

Roads/bridges need to be part of budgetary priorities as long term investments and need to be marketed as such. They are not "sexy" projects, but they drive economic factors and are essential.

problem_land:

Nevertheless, property that was previously large acreages of ranching land or open fields are being developed into neighborhoods and even the medium sized plots of land are being cleared of many trees for single resident developments. The soil is much improved over that in 74012.  My garden was very productive and the soil was barely amended - not so in 74012.

problem_infra:
Our core infrastructure is not being maintained.  Major roads, bridges and highways that we need for good commerce are not being properly prioritized. 

It’s hard asking the electrical question right after we had rolling blackouts and lost electricity.  Nevertheless, before the recent problems in Feb 2021, we have experienced more weather related electrical failure in 74019 than we ever did in 74012 even with more than a decade under our belt in 74012. The push toward renewable energy while also artificially restricting traditional nuclear, coal and gas is a limited and less robust system than a complimenting one that encouraged renewables while not adding obstacles to the traditional energy sources.

problem_water:
Our Payne County rural water district No. 4 has unacceptable levels of something like trihalothalines or something like that.  It says that it is unsafe for elderly people and also for pregnant women and for anyone with a compromised immune system. That just about covers everyone in our area except 5 to 45-year-olds.  We get the water thru Lone Chimney Water Association.  Lone chimney Lake went dry about 8 years ago and our Board negotiated an agreement to buy the water through the Stillwater system which comes from Kaw Lake which takes twice as many chemicals to purify it as did the Lone Chimney Lake water.  Kaw Lake Is up east of Ponca City and is highly polluted from the toxins in the air from Conoco Phillips dropping down into the lake.
Also it is rather well-known that by the time the water travels about halfway to Yale from Stillwater, it has already lost most of the chemicals. We all need to be using rather sophisticated filtering systems in order to drink our own tap water.
Add to that, the water is expensive now and it will only get more expensive. Our rural water bill every month is around $95!
